summary: A country in southeastern South America on the northern shore of the Río de la Plata, with political stability and a well-developed welfare system; it is one of the most secular countries in Latin America and is known for football and beef.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Spain did not found colonial towns in Uruguay until the 18th century, with Montevideo formally established around 1726, and Catholicism arrived with the colonists and later with the great waves of Spanish and Italian immigrants. However, during the colonial period Uruguay was a remote frontier ranching area where the church was far less entrenched than in Peru or Mexico; together with strong secularization policies in the early 20th century, this means that although Catholicism is still the largest religion, its share is among the lowest in Latin America.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Between 1903 and 1915 President José Batlle y Ordóñez pushed radical secularizing reforms: crucifixes were removed from public hospitals in 1906, a divorce law was passed in 1907, church and state were separated in the 1917 constitution, and from 1919 Christmas was renamed "Family Day" and Holy Week "Tourism Week." These policies, together with a high level of education and urbanization, made Uruguay the most secular country in Latin America, with a very high share of people with no religion.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: In 1857 Waldensian Protestants from Piedmont in Italy emigrated to the southwest and founded the "Waldensian Colony"; in the 19th century British merchants also brought Anglicanism and Methodism. Since the 1980s Pentecostal and Evangelical churches have expanded rapidly in working-class neighborhoods, attracting followers by emphasizing miracles and community mutual aid, and the Protestant share has risen markedly.

ranking.name: Others (Judaism, Afro-Brazilian religions, etc.)
ranking.description: The Jewish community originates mainly from immigrants who fled persecution in Eastern Europe and Germany from the early 20th century up to the Second World War, and is concentrated in Montevideo. Afro-Brazilian religions such as Umbanda, from Brazil, arrived in the late 20th century and combined with Uruguay's Afro-Uruguayan culture; every February, at the Festival of Iemanjá, followers make offerings to the sea goddess at the seashore.

religion.background: Uruguay's indigenous Charrúa people were almost exterminated during colonization, and Catholicism arrived with the Spanish colonists and immigrants. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries large numbers of Italian and Spanish immigrants came to Uruguay, while Protestant and Jewish communities also gradually formed. From 1903 President Batlle pursued secularizing reforms, and the separation of church and state in 1917 made Uruguay the most secular country in Latin America. Today the Catholic and non-religious populations are similar in size, while Evangelicals continue to grow.

language.official: The official language is de facto Spanish.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish arrived with Spanish colonization in the 17th-18th centuries; the Spanish spoken in Uruguay is that of the Río de la Plata region, which uses "vos" instead of "tú" to address the other person. Large numbers of Italian immigrants arrived between 1870 and 1930, giving local Spanish an Italian intonation and vocabulary and producing the slang known as "lunfardo." Because the indigenous people nearly vanished in the 19th century and immigrants assimilated quickly, Spanish became the mother tongue of almost the entire population.

ranking.name: Portuguese (Uruguayan Portuguese)
ranking.description: In places in northern Uruguay bordering Brazil, such as Rivera and Artigas, people of Portuguese descent had settled even before the border was fixed in 1828, and a local variety, Uruguayan Portuguese, formed there mixed with Spanish. The education reform pushed by José Pedro Varela in 1877 taught only in Spanish, so this language was long regarded as an "incorrect dialect"; only in recent years has the government begun to recognize its cultural value and promote bilingual education.

language.history: Uruguay's indigenous languages, such as Charrúa, disappeared during colonization, and Spanish has been the main language since the colonial period. Uruguay was once a border zone contested by Spain and Portugal, and so the north retains Portuguese influence. The large-scale European immigration of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, especially Italians, shaped the distinctive accent and slang of Uruguayan Spanish. The national education reform beginning in 1877 spread Spanish throughout the country, and Uruguay has thus become a country with a very high literacy rate.

ranking.name: Asado (Uruguayan barbecue)
ranking.description: Various meats, such as beef short ribs, sausages and offal, are slow-grilled on a grill over embers from burning wood, seasoned only with coarse salt and often served with chimichurri sauce.
ranking.history: In 1611 the colonial official Hernando Arias de Saavedra (Hernandarias) released cattle on the grasslands on the east bank of the Río de la Plata, where the herds multiplied untended and gave rise to the gaucho culture of cattle-based livelihoods. The gauchos' way of grilling beef over a fire in the open is the origin of the Uruguayan asado. Today Uruguay is one of the countries with the highest per-capita beef consumption in the world, and grilling with family and friends on Sundays is regarded as an important ritual of national life.

ranking.name: Chivito (steak sandwich)
ranking.description: Thin steak, ham, cheese, bacon, a fried egg, lettuce and tomato are stuffed into a bread roll, often served with french fries; it is a hearty national sandwich.
ranking.history: It is said that in 1946, in the seaside resort of Punta del Este, an Argentine woman tourist asked the restaurant owner Antonio Carbonaro for a "chivito" (young goat); he had no goat meat on hand, so he substituted steak, ham and butter in bread, which proved very popular and was named "chivito." Ingredients have been added ever since, and the chivito has become Uruguay's most representative fast food.

ranking.name: Milanesa (breaded cutlet)
ranking.description: Thin slices of beef or chicken are coated in beaten egg and breadcrumbs and fried, often squeezed with lemon juice, or topped with tomato sauce and cheese and baked as "a la napolitana."
ranking.history: The milanesa derives from the "cotoletta alla milanese" of Milan, Italy; between 1870 and 1930 large numbers of Italian immigrants came to Uruguay and Argentina and combined it with the abundant beef resources, developing it into an everyday dish that every household makes. Uruguayans often put it in bread as a sandwich or add tomato sauce and cheese. Like pasta and pizza, it reflects the profound influence of Italian immigrants on the food culture of the Río de la Plata.

ranking.name: Dulce de leche
ranking.description: Milk and sugar are cooked slowly over low heat for a long time until they become a thick caramel-colored sauce, which can be spread on bread, used as filling for alfajores or served with all kinds of desserts.
ranking.history: There are many accounts of the exact origin of dulce de leche; in Argentina there is a story that in 1829 a maid simmering milk forgot to turn off the fire and invented it by accident, but similar sweet sauces already existed in colonial Latin America. Both Uruguay and Argentina regard it as a national dessert, and the two countries have even argued with each other over cultural heritage applications. This sauce appears in almost all Uruguayan desserts and is closely tied to the country's well-developed dairy industry.

ranking.name: Yerba mate
ranking.description: Ground yerba mate leaves are put in a gourd cup, hot water is poured in and it is sipped through a metal straw; it tastes slightly bitter and contains caffeine.
ranking.history: Yerba mate was first drunk by the Guaraní indigenous people of South America; in the 17th century the Jesuits began cultivating it on a large scale in their missions in Paraguay, and the gauchos then spread it throughout the Río de la Plata region. Uruguay has the highest per-capita yerba mate consumption in the world, and it is common to see people on the street with a thermos tucked under one arm and a mate cup in hand. Friends sitting in a circle and taking turns drinking from the same mate is a social ritual that symbolizes trust and friendship.
